message.content: Assuming you mean placing the detonator-disguised holocron where the Knights of Ren or Ben Solo would touch it, the idea is more clever than naturally in-character for Hux. Hux would absolutely be threatened if the Knights of Ren became a third party operating outside First Order control. He is insecure, authoritarian, and deeply concerned with command, discipline, and appearances. He would view the Knights not as independent partners, but as a rival power that could embarrass him, bargain with the enemy, or drag the First Order into chaos. What is less Hux-like is the subtle, almost theatrical disguise. He is not usually the kind of officer who patiently constructs a clever trap; he is more likely to use detention, interrogation, security droids, public punishment, or a blunt military kill zone. So the move can work, but only if Hux is not the one personally devising the delicate deception. The trap is clever if it uses Hux’s one real insight: Jedi and Force users often treat relics as symbols, so a fake holocron can become bait for Ben Solo, the Knights, or anyone who needs a piece of Jedi history. A thermal detonator hidden inside a holocron shell is plausible First Order technology, and the cleverness comes from exploiting Force-user assumptions. Hux may not understand the Force, but he understands that Jedi value artifacts, holocrons, and symbolic objects. If he presents the disguised detonator as a recovered holocron, a piece of evidence, a prize, or a relic connected to Ben Solo, it gives the Knights a reason to inspect it, argue over it, or let their guard down. The move is especially smart if it is placed on a table, pedestal, evidence case, or negotiation surface where touching it feels natural. It turns their reverence for Jedi history into a tactical weakness. However, it is not fully in character unless Hux has a reason to know that a holocron would attract the Knights, and unless he can remain ignorant enough to stay true to his personality. Hux is not a Jedi historian, not a Force scholar, and not someone who would casually know which holocron shape, size, or symbol would convince Ben or the Knights. He also would not personally craft a subtle disguise unless forced to do so by pressure, fear, or orders. To make the scene work, have a Force-sensitive officer, a captured Jedi, a droid, or a First Order researcher provide the artifact and the knowledge of how to present it. Hux can still be in character if he simply orders the trap set: “Give them a holocron. If they touch it, remove them.” That keeps him blunt, controlling, and politically motivated, without turning him into a patient schemer. The third-party angle makes the move more plausible because Hux would want the Knights to fail without making the First Order look weak. If the Knights of Ren turn against the First Order as an independent force, Hux would fear they could become a bargaining chip, a rival command, or a source of shame. A disguised thermal detonator gives him a way to destroy them while preserving optics. The incident can be framed as a Jedi trap, a malfunction, an internal security failure, or the Knights’ own recklessness. Hux loves saving face. He would rather claim a security victory than admit that he tried to assassinate Force-sensitive soldiers using a fake relic. This is very in-character because Hux cares deeply about authority, appearances, and being seen as the one who maintains order. The best version of the scene is not Hux as a subtle mastermind, but Hux using a military system to exploit the Knights’ assumptions. Instead of Hux hiding the bomb himself, have him order the disguised holocron placed in a sealed evidence room, a negotiation chamber, a transport crate, or a display case. The detonator should be proximity-triggered, timed, or activated when the wrong Force user touches it. Then Hux can watch from a control room, not because he is a clever Jedi killer, but because he has used bureaucracy, fear, and Force-user ritual to solve a military problem. That is the sweet spot: the move is clever because it uses symbolism, and it is in-character because Hux remains a blunt, controlling, image-obsessed officer rather than a patient schemer.
